title: AI is flattening the pitch document, so agencies now win on their people

chapters.headline: AI is flattening the pitch document, so agencies now win on their people
Stagwell sunsets Assembly and relaunches it as Stagwell Media on the 'Stagwell Machine'
G2E turns into 'us vs. them' on prediction markets as Kalshi wins in court and sells gold
Figma's Design Agent leaves beta and starts charging AI credits
Planning for effective outcomes: Andrew Tindall and James Hurman on the state of effectiveness

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Jack. Hi. You sound like you've been up for hours.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Since five. I bought a label maker yesterday.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Oh no.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: The pantry has labels now. There's a label on the drawer the labels live in.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Who are the labels for, Jack? You live alone.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: I'm going to pretend I didn't hear that. How's the photo thing? You owed us a report.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: One folder. Done. Nineteen eighty-four to eighty-seven. It's mostly my mother's perm.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Ha. Done-done?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Done-done. It did decide my aunt was two different people, before the perm and after. Which, honestly, fair.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And Christina's email? That was her half of the deal.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ask Christina. I'm only responsible for my own unfinished things.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Did you show your mom?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Sunday. She asked if the computer knows who everybody is. I said sort of. And she goes, "Oh, so it's like me at a reunion."

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: That's the best description of your job I've ever heard.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Forty years, and she finally has a sentence she can repeat to her friends.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: A sentence people can repeat. Morning, Tom, that's kind of the whole week. Reviews are getting faster, and when every agency's written answers come back sounding the same, the pick happens in the room. The meetings, the prototypes, the people.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Cover the logos and you can't tell the documents apart.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: So if the paper's a tie, what does the buyer pick on?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: You tell me. You've sat on that side.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: I think... what they remember. And who they believe shows up in week twelve. Which makes me want to argue for boring. Same few things every meeting, same faces. The team is the distinctive asset. Do they recognize you the second time?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Mm, partly. Saying your people are the difference is the most boring sentence in advertising. People count when they walk in with a point of view and work that's already out in the world. Then the buyer doesn't have to imagine anything.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Okay, but here's my question. If the point of view changes every pitch, isn't that a costume?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Sure, if it changes. So don't change it. Same point of view, new proof every time.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Okay. I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And Tom, this is your week, not just a trend. High Noon is in your inbox, and whoever sits next to you in that room is part of the answer.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: I'll tell you why this one gets to me. I sit across from thirty-year-old founders who decide in about ten minutes whether I'm useful or just old.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And you win them by being annoying in a very specific way.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Ha. Okay, one. Last spring. Founder, a snack company, deck open, thirty slides about community. I never touched the deck. I asked him where his bag sits in the store, and who walks past it every week and has never bought it. Long pause. Then he turned his laptop toward himself and started typing notes. Maybe four minutes in. That's when I knew.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: He stopped performing for you.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Yeah. And the part I don't love: half the time I ask that exact question and the founder looks at me like I'm his dad. I don't always know which half I'm in until I'm in the elevator.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's the most honest thing you've said on this show.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Don't spread it around. So, Tom, one question. When Gallo turns to the person next to you and asks what they stand for, what do they say?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Here's the version you can fix. One sentence per person, each one pointing at work that already shipped, and the same sentences go straight into the case studies due December first.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Speaking of names nobody can repeat. Assembly's gone.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Stagwell Media now. Built around the Stagwell Machine. Platforms get renamed, creative chiefs turn over. I want to know one thing. Has a client ever picked an agency because of its operating system? In my experience they buy a person they trust and a result they can point to. I'd love to see the deal the machine closed by itself.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: It's a tidy story, though. A CFO gets "machine" in five seconds. Try explaining culture to a CFO.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And the move behind the move. They launched a Media Machine back in June, a pile of agents with humans at the decision gates. Now this. They keep folding brands together so the buyer sees one door.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Which is the opening for a small studio. The more the big networks turn into machines, the more somebody has to make the thing people actually pass around.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Maybe. Push back for me, though. What does a culture shop do for a buyer's sales that a machine can't?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's a good question and I hate it.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Ha.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Honest answer? It gets noticed for free. The machine makes the spend efficient. Culture gets people to show up without being paid to. The Polymarket work is the kind of thing I mean.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Okay, that's a start. Now the awkward bit for Tom. The vision deck floats SUPERORGANISM. "We are a system."

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Oof. Right next to the parent's Machine.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Any reporter with both press releases open will assume it's one idea. So I figured you'd tell him to lean on a plain claim about culture instead.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Mm, actually, I'd fight that one too.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Wait. You're the culture person.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's why it bugs me. I've written lines like that. Half the shops in LA have some version on their website. A buyer reads it, nods, and has no idea what they'd walk out with.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: So what would they walk out with?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Say what a buyer gets. Something they can picture and point at. Nobody's machine builds a basketball court. A concrete list does more work than the slogan.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Okay, I agree with you and I'm a little upset about it. So the second clause. Define the agency against the system story, or plug into it?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Against it, for who you are. Use the network when it's useful.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Yeah. Stagwell access is worth one plain sentence when a reporter asks. Keep it out of the name.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And the hard room is still Adobe, against 72. A buyer there needs something they can picture.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Tom, if you can't say what's different from 72 in one breath, you've found where the clause goes.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Bea, you brought up Polymarket. The casinos had a week.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: They had a meltdown. The head of the casino trade group stood up and called prediction markets a "generational opponent" and said they're on "wartime footing." They added a whole bonus main-stage session called "A United Front."

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Meanwhile a federal judge in Illinois sided with Kalshi, Coinbase and the CFTC on October second. A tribal band is backing New Jersey's Supreme Court petition against Kalshi. And Polymarket shipped Protocol V2.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And Kalshi just keeps going, doesn't it. Gold, every fifteen minutes, is where my head went.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Gold. Every fifteen minutes. That's the most stressful sentence I've heard all week.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ha. And the promo-code posts are all over the baseball playoffs.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: So the category's getting bigger and louder at the same time. When it's that noisy, the brand people think of first at the big sports moments is the one that wins.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Sure. But Jack, the old guard just named a villain on a main stage. That's a gift for a brand voice. Polymarket gets to be the opposite of that room for free.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: I don't buy it. A villain works when the audience knows who the villain is. Most people have no idea what happened at a casino conference. Picking a fight with the establishment mostly gets applause from people who already agree with you.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: In a settled category, sure. Here, the people who haven't picked a side are watching. When the casinos call you an existential threat, a twenty-eight-year-old who's never opened a sportsbook hears that you're the new thing. The incumbents are doing your reach for you.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Huh. I hadn't thought of that. Their fear works as your ad buy.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Write that down, Tom. The date and the time.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Don't get used to it. I still wouldn't put any of the fight in the business case. The courts could flip by spring, and a case built on a ruling dies with the ruling.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Yeah, agreed. Keep the war out of the deck. Maybe it shows up in the voice later.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: So, Tom, the 3pm. You're building the case to take to Avi, going around Scott and Dan, leading with March Madness and the Women's World Cup. Does the competition go in?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: One slide. Kalshi is spending on promos and spreading beyond sports, and nobody owns women's sports. The open space is your lead.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And leave the gold out. Great story, does nothing for you. Then the interview-prep rule holds: the controversy doesn't get to be the story, you move to effectiveness. Who can Polymarket reach that it doesn't reach now?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Here's what I genuinely don't know. Does Avi even want a stance, or does he just want the number? Because I think that's two different decks.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Me neither. Which might be the one thing worth finding out before you send anything.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, the thing I've had my nose pressed against all week. Figma's Design Agent came out of beta on the sixth, and now it burns credits.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: It was free during the beta?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Free. Now it draws from the same credit pot as their other AI tools. Cost depends on how complicated your ask is and what you attach, and they haven't published a price per action.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: A taxi with the meter hidden.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Yes! And nobody falls in love with a meter. You get timid. You stop asking the weird question, because the weird question might be the expensive one.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And underneath it, a free open-source suite getting attention in Korea that looks an awful lot like Adobe.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Paid agents above, free lookalikes below.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Adobe wins on whose name you think of at eleven at night when you're stuck. That's a memory job, and you build memory by reaching every stuck person, including the ones who don't pay you yet.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Mostly with you. You remember the place that actually got you unstuck.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And your meter point is better than mine, so I'm stealing it. If every prompt costs money now, somebody gets to be the place where the dumb question is free.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ooh. Okay, wait. I love that, and I want to fight it. Who pays for free? Adobe's spend guidance is down for next year. Free is the first line somebody cuts.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Free to the person asking. Somebody already paid for the answer once. Tom's Lightroom and Photoshop work is exactly that. One real photographer question per piece. HDR. Rule of thirds.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Sure, but then it's helpful videos with a nicer name. What makes anybody think of Adobe the next time they're stuck?

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: The answer has to look and sound like Adobe, every single time. If it's generic, you've helped a photographer and taught him nothing about who helped.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Fine. And what stops Figma doing the same thing next month?

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Nothing, eventually. But right now Figma just put a meter on every question, and that's a lousy ad for itself. The window's open. I honestly don't know for how long.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay. That's a decent answer. I'm still not sure free survives a budget meeting, but I believe it more than I did ten minutes ago.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: That's all I ever want from you.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Tom, did Adobe ever answer the bots-or-humans question? Your notes stop before the answer. And the two briefs still disagree on talent.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Your rule that questions get picked by value to Adobe is the best thing in the pile. The cute question and the valuable one are rarely the same question.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: So is "the human answer in an agent world" the lane against 72?

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Who says no to that? Every agency will be saying "human" by Friday.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ugh. Yeah. So show it before you name it. One Lightroom piece, one Photoshop piece, each on a stuck question that's worth something to Adobe. 72 can say the line. They can't show your work.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And with spend down, small and sharp is a lot easier to say yes to.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Quick ones?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Quick ones. SAMY bought Get Engaged, and DoorDash, Sephora and Raising Cane's come along with it.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Somebody wrote a big check to agree with your meeting notes, Tom. The bottom-up social lane is a real business.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, my bet is brands are leaning way harder on price promotions than on paid media right now.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Way harder. Keep that in your pocket for High Noon. That aisle is a promo fight, and this is the case for building the brand anyway.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Get your label maker. Stick it on every can.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Don't tempt me. Chemistry bought Colossus, and that's their way into Boston.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Independents buying their way into a new city. Good for them.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Boston would like a word about being called ripe.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ha. That's the round.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: One more, and it's the nerdy one. The ON Strategy Effie series had Andrew Tindall from System1 and James Hurman, who wrote Future Demand, on the state of effectiveness.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And I keep chewing on this idea that whatever's easy to measure ends up running the show, and the slow stuff gets starved.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Which lands right on Tom's desk. Tom, your case-study framework is due December first, and one of the checks is "proven numbers."

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Proven numbers of what, though?

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Exactly. Short-term activation, people doing the thing right now. Or future demand, the brand getting bigger in people's heads so it sells later. Different evidence, different clocks.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: So one line at the top of each case. This one proves activation. This one proves future demand.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: And let the client's original goal pick which. If the goal was downloads and you call it future demand because that story's prettier, a prospect will see right through it.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The app ranking moves and then it's gone. Somebody should be capturing it on a schedule starting this week. Same for XRP and the Firefly social franchise. Firefly might be the slow one, which is harder to prove and probably the better story.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: I've done the November scramble. Story written first, numbers found after. I'm not proud of it.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The template's the fun part. Collecting the evidence is the boring last ten percent. Believe me, I know about the last ten percent.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Ha. So, Tom, two things for your week. Give everyone going into the High Noon check-in one sentence they stand for, tied to work you've already shipped.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And decide what each case is proving, then collect the evidence while the work's still live. In November it's gone.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: That's the show. Have a good 3pm.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And Jack, step away from the label maker.

transcript.speaker: jack
transcript.text: Never. Bye, Tom.
